Water dissociation at solid surfaces underpins processes ranging from corrosion and
catalysis to electrochemistry and photovoltaics. Defects often serve as reactive sites
for dissociation, yet how solvation influences water dissociation at such sites remains
poorly understood. Here, we use state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic poten-
tials to explore water dissociation at defective graphene-water interfaces. We show that
solvation qualitatively changes the reaction mechanism at a graphene single vacancy
(SV), opening pathways that are absent for an isolated water molecule. Whereas the
gas-phase process proceeds via a single concerted channel, the solvated SV splits wa-
ter through two competing pathways: a basic route forming SV-H and OH–
an acidic route forming SV-OH and H3O+

distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene-water adsorption. Accord-
ingly, even a simple carbon vacancy gives rise to unexpectedly rich interfacial chemistry,
coupling surface chemistry to interfacial charge and wettability, with implications for
carbon functionalization and nanofluidic transport.

The dissociation of water at a solid surface is a fundamental elementary reaction step in
chemistry.1,2 In the gas phase, it takes 5 eV to cleave an O-H bond;3 however, when in
contact with a surface, this process can proceed at a fraction of the energetic cost, with
reported barriers often below 1 eV.4 Surface-mediated water dissociation underpins several
key processes, including the Volmer step of alkaline hydrogen evolution,5 the water-gas shift
reaction,6 and photocatalytic water splitting.7,8 Left unchecked, the same chemistry corrodes
carbon electrodes in fuel cells and degrades metal and oxide surfaces exposed to aqueous
environments.9 Whether a given surface dissociates water, and by which mechanism, depends
sensitively on the electronic structure of the surface, its local coordination and geometry, and
the hydrogen-bonding environment provided by the surrounding water.2,10
There are a number of mechanisms by which water dissociates at a surface. On flat tran-
sition metals, water molecules can undergo direct dissociative chemisorption, colliding with
the metal surface and cleaving an O-H bond to deposit H and OH fragments via a concerted
mechanism.10 Solvation with other water molecules can facilitate this process.11,12 When
corrugations, steps, or kinks are introduced to the surface, metal-water dissociation can be
further enhanced with binding to undercoordinated sites.13–15 On metal oxide surfaces such
as rutile TiO2(110), oxygen vacancies can help promote dissociation via heterolytic mech-
anisms in which a proton transfers to a neighboring surface oxygen, yielding two surface
hydroxyls per defect.16,17 The surrounding solvent can also play an important role; in the
case of pristine TiO2, water dissociation can proceed through solvent-assisted proton transfer
pathways that vary from one-step to two-step processes depending on the facet.18–21 Similar
proton-transfer phenomena occur at solvated ZnO surfaces.22 Yet, while defect-mediated re-
activity and solvent-assisted proton transfer are well-established for metals and metal oxides,
how these two phenomena couple together for 2D materials such as graphene, MoS2, or hBN
remains far less understood.23–28
These gaps motivate two key open questions: (i) how does solvation alter the mecha-
nism and energetics of water dissociation for these 2D materials, and (ii) how do the resulting

To address these questions, we begin by characterizing graphene surfaces, which are
widely used in membranes, electrodes, and nanofluidic devices in permanent contact with
liquid water. Under pristine conditions, graphene does not dissociate water due to weak
graphene-water interactions.29 Under realistic operating conditions, however, graphene is
not a pristine sheet of regularly repeating carbon atoms; it contains vacancies and edge
sites that arise during synthesis, from chemical reactions, or from ionizing radiation.30–32
These defects have been observed experimentally33–37 and are known to alter the electronic,
mechanical, and chemical properties of the graphene sheet.38–40 One of the most important
of these defects is the graphene single vacancy (SV), a diradical with two unpaired electrons
(spin moment = 2µB) created by removing a single carbon atom at a cost of 7.9 eV.41,42 One

of its unpaired electrons is located in a localized σ orbital (−2.4 eV), while the other resides
in an out-of-plane π orbital (−1.1 eV)(see Figure 1a).41,43–45 Together these defect states
make the SV an effective reactive center, capable of both donating and accepting electron
density from an incoming adsorbate – a Janus-style defect. For the case of water dissociation,
gas-phase density functional theory (DFT) calculations have confirmed that single water
molecules chemisorb at the SV, proceeding through a concerted transition state to form a
series of increasingly stable products.46–48 This overall chemisorption process is shown in
Figure 1b. Water first attacks the bare vacancy and forms a Hydroxy-SV species containing
C–OH and C–H groups. The OH group then transfers a proton to the remaining carbon with
a dangling bond to form a SV-Ketone species. Finally, this ketone undergoes reorganization
to form a SV-Pyran motif. Overall, the SV + H2O reaction is highly exothermic, with the
final products being roughly 100 kcal/mol more stable than the bare SV and physisorbed
water.
The dissociation of a single water molecule at the graphene SV is understood.46–48 How-
ever, a description of this process under bulk solvation conditions is missing. This is notable
given the capacity for surrounding water molecules to alter both the mechanism and ener-
getics of surface water dissociation.11,12,18,22 Traditional DFT approaches, which have been
used extensively to characterize the gas-phase SV reactivity, are too costly for modeling fully
solvated systems over the nanosecond simulation times required for enhanced sampling. Clas-
sical force fields, meanwhile, cannot adequately describe bond-making and bond-breaking.
To overcome these limitations, we train a MACE interatomic potential on spin-polarized
hybrid DFT data – specifically, revPBE0-D3 – to run enhanced-sampling simulations. Hy-
brid DFT is essential for this goal. Semi-local functionals suffer more severely from self-
interaction errors that cause delocalized π bands to cross the Fermi level, artificially re-
ducing the magnetization from its expected value of 2 µB (see Figures S1 and S2 of the
Supporting Information).41 Combining our machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP)
with multiple-walker well-tempered metadynamics, we enable multi-nanosecond trajectories
5

of complex, reactive vacancy systems at a spin-polarized hybrid DFT level of theory (see
Computational Methods for details).
We characterize the SV + H2O reaction by computing 2D free energy surfaces as a
function of the collective variables sCH and sCO, which track the coordination of the SV site
to hydrogen and oxygen atoms, respectively (see Computational Methods for more details).
These free energy surfaces are shown in Figures 2b and 2c, with the relevant minima and
transition states shown as state-energy profiles in Figure 2d. For this analysis, we show the
dissociation process only up to the SV-Ketone state: this species is kinetically stabilized
under ambient conditions, separated from the thermodynamically more stable SV-Pyran
by a forward free energy barrier of ∼45 kcal/mol.
This final SV-Ketone →SV-Pyran
transformation is therefore treated separately in Figure S5 of the Supporting Information.
The gaseous reaction presents a relatively simple free energy landscape, with a single
reaction channel connecting the bare SV to the chemisorbed product (Figure 2b/d). Water
attacks the vacancy over a 28.4 kcal/mol barrier in a concerted step that simultaneously
breaks an O–H bond and forms C–OH and C–H bonds at the defect site, yielding the
Hydroxy-SV intermediate. This step is rate-limiting for the dissociation process, and the
Hydroxy-SV easily decomposes to form the SV-Ketone over a very small barrier. Overall,
gaseous water dissociation is strongly exergonic, with the SV-Ketone lying 78 kcal/mol below
the bare SV + H2O reactant. This value is ∼13 kcal/mol smaller in magnitude than the
potential energy difference (∆E ∼91 kcal/mol, see Figure S4), a difference that we can
attribute to the entropic cost of immobilising a free molecule at the surface.49
The solvated free energy landscape is more intricate (see Figure 2c/d). Two distinct
reaction channels now connect the bare SV to the chemisorbed products, corresponding to
two modes of water attack on the vacancy:

anism): Single step dissociative adsorption. Bottom (solvated mechanisms): Dissociative

In the first pathway, the SV abstracts a proton from the nearby water to form an SV–
H intermediate and an adjacent solvated hydroxide ion. In the second, water attacks the
vacancy oxygen-first to form SV–OH, transferring one of its protons to the surrounding
media via the Grotthus mechanism. Both processes occur with comparable forward free
energy barriers – indicative of an early transition state governed primarily by O–H bond
cleavage – but with the SV–OH/H3O+ intermediate being ∼20 kcal/mol more stable in free
energy. These forward barriers (21.9 kcal/mol for SV–H/OH– formation, and 23.7 kcal/mol
for SV–OH/H3O+) are overall lower in free energy than for the concerted gas-phase process
(28.4 kcal/mol). From either intermediate, the system proceeds to the Hydroxy-SV and then
to the SV-Ketone, which lies 74 kcal/mol below the solvated bare SV.
The contrast between gaseous and solvated water dissociation arises directly from the
surrounding liquid. Solvent molecules stabilize the charged H3O+ and OH– fragments through
hydrogen bonding and dielectric screening, opening up heterolytic reaction channels that
have no gas-phase counterpart. Under gaseous conditions, where no charge stabilization is

possible, dissociation proceeds through a concerted transition state that forces a hydrogen
atom through the graphene plane. The overall reaction mechanisms for gaseous and solvated
water dissociation are shown in Figure 3. The dual reactivity of the solvated Janus-like SV,
accepting either the hydrogen or the hydroxyl fragment of the dissociating water molecule, is
reminiscent of the ambiphilic character of carbenes in molecular chemistry.50 The graphene
SV possesses a similar pair of σ and π orbitals, and in this sense acts as a surface analogue
of molecular carbenes. The greater energetic stability of the SV-OH intermediate over SV-H
suggests that the acidic pathway is thermodynamically favored, which may produce a local
excess of hydronium ions at the defect sites. This chemical contribution to interfacial acidity
would add to the proton accumulation already observed at pristine graphene surfaces.51
The competing chemisorption pathways highlight the important contribution of solvent
molecules to surface water dissociation. The result is a series of structurally distinct interme-
diates, each presenting different functional groups to the solvent that modify the local water
environment in different ways. We investigate this using 2D adsorption profiles and water res-
idence lifetimes, which are shown in Figure 4. Hydrogen bonding between the chemisorbed
groups and the surrounding liquid is the primary impetus of enhanced water adsorption,
consistent with previous ab initio molecular dynamics studies of defective graphene-water
interfaces.26 The effect is strongly product-dependent. The Hydroxy-SV (τ = 55 ps) and
SV-Ketone (τ = 27 ps) states, both of which present hydrogen-bond-active O–H or C=O
groups to the liquid, display water residence times several times greater than either the bare
SV or the SV-Pyran, which are comparable to the pristine graphene lifetime. Chemisorption
therefore not only transforms the local electronic structure of the defect, but also converts
it from a hydrophobic to a hydrophilic site while simultaneously passivating the SV against
further chemical attack from water. This suggests that controlled defect chemistry could
offer a route to modulating wettability and friction at graphene–water interfaces, and that
quantitative modeling of these phenomena requires moving beyond the pristine graphene
approximation.

In conclusion, we show that solvation qualitatively transforms the mechanism of water disso-
ciation at defects. Whereas the gas-phase reaction proceeds via a single concerted channel,
solvated dissociation is a bimodal, stepwise process in which the surrounding liquid stabilizes
charged intermediates and opens heterolytic pathways that are absent in vacuum. These sol-
vated reaction routes offer lower forward barriers and yield chemisorbed products that, in
turn, enhance local water adsorption at the defect site.
Our work highlights the importance of explicit solvation in simulating reactive interfacial
chemical systems. This has been established for metals and metal oxides, but our results
10

demonstrate that it extends to 2D carbon surfaces, where a single atomic vacancy is sufficient
to transform the local environment from physisorption to reactive chemisorption. The two
Janus-like acidic and basic pathways identified here, as well as the thermodynamic preference
for the acidic channel, suggest that solvated graphene vacancies may act as short-lived, local
sources of hydronium, contributing to interfacial acidity beyond what is observed at pris-
tine graphene surfaces.51 More broadly, direct comparisons between gas-phase and solvated
water dissociation remain rare for any surface. The qualitative changes we observe, i.e.,
solvation opening competing ionic channels, stabilizing intermediates, and lowering barriers,
are unlikely to be unique to carbon and may require reassessment of reaction mechanisms
previously characterized only under vacuum conditions. We expect that these effects will also
be relevant to other 2D material interfaces, for example, for monolayer hBN which exhibits
strong surface charging effects.24
Looking forward, the distinct states identified here, each with different water adsorption
properties and residence times, suggest that controlled defect engineering could offer a route
to tuning wettability, friction, and selective ion transport in 2D-membrane materials. An
important next step is to understand cooperative effects and whether proximal vacancies
react independently or exhibit coupled reactivity that could be exploited for selective surface
chemistry.40 More generally, our work demonstrates that machine-learned potentials trained
on hybrid DFT, combined with enhanced-sampling techniques, now make it feasible to resolve
the full free energy landscape of rare reactive events at explicitly solvated interfaces. This
approach is readily transferable to other defective 2D materials and reactive solid–liquid
systems.
Computational Methods
In this work, we develop an equivariant MACE potential at a hybrid DFT level of theory.
Training structures were generated using exhaustive sampling through the use of foundation
MACE models (MP0),52 through AIMD, and from preliminary NEB and umbrella integra-
11

tion runs. In total, around 9000 structures were generated, with configurations including
defects under solvated, partially solvated, and gaseous conditions. For each configuration,
single-point DFT calculations were performed using FHI-aims.53–55 Spin-unrestricted Kohn-
Sham calculations were used for configurations containing undercoordinated carbon atoms;
spin-restricted calculations were used otherwise. In this way, we selected the lowest-energy
electronic states such that we were sampling the adiabatic energy surface. For SV and other
triplet-state calculations, initial magnetizations of 0.5 −1.0 µB were applied to the three
nearest carbon atoms surrounding the vacancy site. Hybrid calculations were performed
using the revPBE0 functional augmented by Grimme’s D3 corrections (zero damping).56–59
For these calculations, we employed the intermediate orbital basis with a 4 × 4 × 1 k-grid.
The MACE potential was generated via a two-step procedure. First, a base model was
generated at a GGA level of theory (revPBE-D3,56,57,59 ∼7000 labeled structures). This
model was then transfer-learned to the revPBE0-D3 level via transfer learning on a smaller
subset of labeled structures (∼2000). This final hybrid-level MACE model was generated
with 128 channels and a maximal message equivariance of L = 1. A radial cutoff of 5 ˚A was
selected, which equates to an effective receptive field of 10 ˚A after message passing. The
final model exhibited training RMSEs of 1.3 meV/atom and 30.6 meV/˚A for the energies
and forces, respectively.
Model performance was evaluated through force error analysis
(see Figure S3) and through NEB calculations across the water dissociation pathway, where
MACE energies and barriers agree with those of revPBE0-D3 reference values to within
2 −3 kcal/mol (see Figure S4).
Well-tempered metadynamics was performed by coupling LAMMPS with the multiple-
walker setup available in PLUMED.60–64 For the gas-phase reaction, 4 walkers were initialized
from various states spanning the reaction coordinate using a 12.350 ˚A × 12.834 ˚A × 30.000 ˚A
simulation cell containing a single water molecule (see Figure 2a). For the solvated reaction,
8 walkers were similarly initialized using a 12.350 ˚A × 12.834 ˚A × 36.000 ˚A cell containing
∼60 water molecules (see Figure 2a). Simulations were performed using the NVT ensemble
12

(Nos´e-Hoover-style) at 300 K and with a time constant of 100 fs.
The individual time
step was set to 0.5 fs.
We chose two collective variables to probe this reaction: a C-H
coordination number that tracks the number of hydrogens bound at the single vacancy;
and a C-O coordination number that tracks the number of oxygen atoms bound at the
site. Restraints were appropriately applied to restrict reaction to a single water molecule
at any one time reacting directly at the single vacancy. Some side reactions were observed
during the course of these simulations (e.g., oxygen slipping onto an adjacent, non-defect
carbon) but these did not perturb the defects state energies and minima under consideration.
Convergence of the metadynamics runs was monitored by tracking the relative free energies of
the various chemisorbed states. In total, the gaseous and solvated metadynamics simulations
were run for a cumulative time of 6 ns and 40 ns, respectively. Unbiased NV T simulations,
used to characterize the physisorption of water at the graphene defects, were performed
over 2 ns using extended simulation cells (17.290 ˚A × 17.112 ˚A × 45.00 ˚A) consisting of
∼160 water molecules (see Figure 4a). The following correlation function c(t) was used to
analyze water adsorption and residence times: c(t) = ⟨h(0)h(t)⟩/⟨h⟩where h is 1 for a water
adsorbed at the defect site (within 3.5 ˚A of the defect atoms) and 0 otherwise.

2609.11602::problem_motivation::0.evidence_span: Defects often serve as reactive sites for dissociation, yet how solvation influences water dissociation at such sites remains poorly understood.

2609.11602::problem_motivation::1.evidence_span: Yet, while defect-mediated reactivity and solvent-assisted proton transfer are well-established for metals and metal oxides, how these two phenomena couple together for 2D materials such as graphene, MoS2, or hBN remains far less understood.

2609.11602::problem_motivation::2.evidence_span: These gaps motivate two key open questions: (i) how does solvation alter the mechanism and energetics of water dissociation for these 2D materials, and (ii) how do the resulting chemisorbed species modify the structure and adsorption properties of the surrounding water?

2609.11602::problem_motivation::3.evidence_span: However, a description of this process under bulk solvation conditions is missing.

2609.11602::problem_motivation::4.evidence_span: More broadly, direct comparisons between gas-phase and solvated water dissociation remain rare for any surface.

2609.11602::problem_motivation::5.evidence_span: An important next step is to understand cooperative effects and whether proximal vacancies react independently or exhibit coupled reactivity

2609.11602::prior_approach::0.evidence_span: On flat transition metals, water molecules can undergo direct dissociative chemisorption, colliding with the metal surface and cleaving an O-H bond to deposit H and OH fragments via a concerted mechanism.
Solvation with other water molecules can facilitate this process.
When corrugations, steps, or kinks are introduced to the surface, metal-water dissociation can be further enhanced with binding to undercoordinated sites.

On metal oxide surfaces such as rutile TiO2(110), oxygen vacancies can help promote dissociation via heterolytic mechanisms in which a proton transfers to a neighboring surface oxygen, yielding two surface hydroxyls per defect.
in the case of pristine TiO2, water dissociation can proceed through solvent-assisted proton transfer pathways that vary from one-step to two-step processes depending on the facet.
Similar proton-transfer phenomena occur at solvated ZnO surfaces.

2609.11602::prior_approach::1.evidence_span: Under pristine conditions, graphene does not dissociate water due to weak graphene-water interactions.

2609.11602::prior_approach::2.evidence_span: For the case of water dissociation, gas-phase density functional theory (DFT) calculations have confirmed that single water molecules chemisorb at the SV, proceeding through a concerted transition state to form a series of increasingly stable products.
consistent with previous ab initio molecular dynamics studies of defective graphene-water interfaces.

2609.11602::prior_limitation::0.evidence_span: Traditional DFT approaches, which have been used extensively to characterize the gas-phase SV reactivity, are too costly for modeling fully solvated systems over the nanosecond simulation times required for enhanced sampling.
Classical force fields, meanwhile, cannot adequately describe bond-making and bond-breaking.

2609.11602::rejected_alternative::0.evidence_span: Semi-local functionals suffer more severely from self-interaction errors that cause delocalized π bands to cross the Fermi level, artificially reducing the magnetization from its expected value of 2 µB
quantitative modeling of these phenomena requires moving beyond the pristine graphene approximation.

2609.11602::inspiration_source::0.evidence_span: The dual reactivity of the solvated Janus-like SV, accepting either the hydrogen or the hydroxyl fragment of the dissociating water molecule, is reminiscent of the ambiphilic character of carbenes in molecular chemistry.

2609.11602::causal_claim::0.evidence_span: We show that solvation qualitatively changes the reaction mechanism at a graphene single vacancy (SV), opening pathways that are absent for an isolated water molecule.)

Whereas the gas-phase process proceeds via a single concerted channel, the solvated SV splits water through two competing pathways: a basic route forming SV-H and OH– an acidic route forming SV-OH and H3O+ (aq).)

solvated dissociation is a bimodal, stepwise process in which the surrounding liquid stabilizes charged intermediates and opens heterolytic pathways that are absent in vacuum. These solvated reaction routes offer lower forward barriers)

2609.11602::causal_claim::1.evidence_span: These lower-barrier pathways produce distinct chemisorbed intermediates that enhance graphene-water adsorption.)
Hydrogen bonding between the chemisorbed groups and the surrounding liquid is the primary impetus of enhanced water adsorption)

2609.11602::causal_claim::2.evidence_span: Water first attacks the bare vacancy and forms a Hydroxy-SV species containing C–OH and C–H groups.)
The OH group then transfers a proton to the remaining carbon with a dangling bond to form a SV-Ketone species.)
Finally, this ketone undergoes reorganization to form a SV-Pyran motif.)

2609.11602::causal_claim::3.evidence_span: a single atomic vacancy is sufficient to transform the local environment from physisorption to reactive chemisorption.)

Chemisorption therefore not only transforms the local electronic structure of the defect, but also converts it from a hydrophobic to a hydrophilic site while simultaneously passivating the SV against further chemical attack from water.)

2609.11602::causal_claim::4.evidence_span: These defects have been observed experimentally and are known to alter the electronic, mechanical, and chemical properties of the graphene sheet.)

2609.11602::causal_claim::5.evidence_span: Combining our machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) with multiple-walker well-tempered metadynamics, we enable multi-nanosecond trajectories of complex, reactive vacancy systems at a spin-polarized hybrid DFT level of theory)

our work demonstrates that machine-learned potentials trained on hybrid DFT, combined with enhanced-sampling techniques, now make it feasible to resolve the full free energy landscape of rare reactive events at explicitly solvated interfaces.)

2609.11602::mechanism_principle::0.evidence_span: Whether a given surface dissociates water, and by which mechanism, depends sensitively on the electronic structure of the surface, its local coordination and geometry, and the hydrogen-bonding environment provided by the surrounding water.

2609.11602::mechanism_principle::1.evidence_span: The graphene SV possesses a similar pair of σ and π orbitals, and in this sense acts as a surface analogue of molecular carbenes.
Together these defect states make the SV an effective reactive center, capable of both donating and accepting electron density from an incoming adsorbate – a Janus-style defect.

2609.11602::mechanism_principle::2.evidence_span: a difference that we can attribute to the entropic cost of immobilising a free molecule at the surface.

2609.11602::mechanism_principle::3.evidence_span: The contrast between gaseous and solvated water dissociation arises directly from the surrounding liquid. Solvent molecules stabilize the charged H3O+ and OH– fragments through hydrogen bonding and dielectric screening, opening up heterolytic reaction channels that have no gas-phase counterpart.
Under gaseous conditions, where no charge stabilization is possible, dissociation proceeds through a concerted transition state that forces a hydrogen atom through the graphene plane.

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::0.evidence_span: To overcome these limitations, we train a MACE interatomic potential on spin-polarized hybrid DFT data – specifically, revPBE0-D3 – to run enhanced-sampling simulations.

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::1.evidence_span: The greater energetic stability of the SV-OH intermediate over SV-H suggests that the acidic pathway is thermodynamically favored, which may produce a local excess of hydronium ions at the defect sites.

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::2.evidence_span: This suggests that controlled defect chemistry could offer a route to modulating wettability and friction at graphene–water interfaces

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::3.evidence_span: suggest that solvated graphene vacancies may act as short-lived, local sources of hydronium, contributing to interfacial acidity beyond what is observed at pristine graphene surfaces.

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::4.evidence_span: The qualitative changes we observe, i.e., solvation opening competing ionic channels, stabilizing intermediates, and lowering barriers, are unlikely to be unique to carbon and may require reassessment of reaction mechanisms previously characterized only under vacuum conditions.

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::5.evidence_span: We expect that these effects will also be relevant to other 2D material interfaces, for example, for monolayer hBN which exhibits strong surface charging effects.

2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::6.evidence_span: controlled defect engineering could offer a route to tuning wettability, friction, and selective ion transport in 2D-membrane materials.

2609.11602::evidence_result::0.evidence_span: Overall, the SV + H2O reaction is highly exothermic, with the final products being roughly 100 kcal/mol more stable than the bare SV and physisorbed water.
Overall, gaseous water dissociation is strongly exergonic, with the SV-Ketone lying 78 kcal/mol below the bare SV + H2O reactant.
From either intermediate, the system proceeds to the Hydroxy-SV and then to the SV-Ketone, which lies 74 kcal/mol below the solvated bare SV.

2609.11602::evidence_result::1.evidence_span: The gaseous reaction presents a relatively simple free energy landscape, with a single reaction channel connecting the bare SV to the chemisorbed product

Water attacks the vacancy over a 28.4 kcal/mol barrier in a concerted step that simultaneously breaks an O–H bond and forms C–OH and C–H bonds at the defect site, yielding the Hydroxy-SV intermediate.
the Hydroxy-SV easily decomposes to form the SV-Ketone over a very small barrier.

2609.11602::evidence_result::2.evidence_span: The solvated free energy landscape is more intricate (see Figure 2c/d). Two distinct reaction channels now connect the bare SV to the chemisorbed products)
In the first pathway, the SV abstracts a proton from the nearby water to form an SV–H intermediate and an adjacent solvated hydroxide ion.
In the second, water attacks the vacancy oxygen-first to form SV–OH, transferring one of its protons to the surrounding media via the Grotthus mechanism.

Both processes occur with comparable forward free energy barriers – indicative of an early transition state governed primarily by O–H bond cleavage – but with the SV–OH/H3O+ intermediate being ∼20 kcal/mol more stable in free energy.
These forward barriers (21.9 kcal/mol for SV–H/OH– formation, and 23.7 kcal/mol for SV–OH/H3O+) are overall lower in free energy than for the concerted gas-phase process (28.4 kcal/mol).
From either intermediate, the system proceeds to the Hydroxy-SV and then to the SV-Ketone, which lies 74 kcal/mol below the solvated bare SV.

2609.11602::evidence_result::3.evidence_span: The Hydroxy-SV (τ = 55 ps) and SV-Ketone (τ = 27 ps) states, both of which present hydrogen-bond-active O–H or C=O groups to the liquid, display water residence times several times greater than either the bare SV or the SV-Pyran, which are comparable to the pristine graphene lifetime.
and yield chemisorbed products that, in turn, enhance local water adsorption at the defect site.

2609.11602::evidence_result::4.evidence_span: The final model exhibited training RMSEs of 1.3 meV/atom and 30.6 meV/˚A for the energies and forces, respectively.
MACE energies and barriers agree with those of revPBE0-D3 reference values to within 2 −3 kcal/mol

2609.11602::constraint::0.evidence_span: For this analysis, we show the dissociation process only up to the SV-Ketone state: this species is kinetically stabilized under ambient conditions, separated from the thermodynamically more stable SV-Pyran by a forward free energy barrier of ∼45 kcal/mol.

2609.11602::constraint::1.evidence_span: Spin-unrestricted Kohn-Sham calculations were used for configurations containing undercoordinated carbon atoms; spin-restricted calculations were used otherwise.

2609.11602::constraint::2.evidence_span: In this way, we selected the lowest-energy electronic states such that we were sampling the adiabatic energy surface.

2609.11602::constraint::3.evidence_span: Restraints were appropriately applied to restrict reaction to a single water molecule at any one time reacting directly at the single vacancy.
